title: Stationary Waves
short_init: Stationary or standing waves are formed by the superposition of two identical waves traveling in opposite directions along the same line. They are characterized by regions of zero amplitude called nodes and maximum amplitude called antinodes.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Superposition principle, formation of stationary waves, nodes and antinodes, characteristics of standing waves, standing waves in strings (fundamental frequency and harmonics), and open and closed organ pipes.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Analytical treatment of reflection from fixed and free boundaries, phase change on reflection, energy density and energy transmission in stationary waves, organ pipes with end corrections, resonance column apparatus, and Melde's experiment.

prerequisites: Boundary conditions for strings and air columns

concept_notes.heading: Formation and Characteristics of Stationary Waves
bullets: Formed when an incident wave interferes with its reflected counterpart of equal amplitude and frequency.
Energy is not propagated along the medium; it is localized between nodes, leading to standing patterns.
All particles between two successive nodes vibrate in phase with each other, though with different amplitudes.

concept_notes.heading: Nodes and Antinodes
bullets: Nodes are points of permanent zero displacement and maximum pressure/stress variation.
Antinodes are points of maximum displacement amplitude and minimum pressure/stress variation.
The separation between consecutive nodes or consecutive antinodes is lambda / 2, while between a node and its adjacent antinode it is lambda / 4.

concept_notes.heading: Stationary Waves in Stretched Strings
bullets: A string fixed at both ends supports transverse standing waves with nodes at the fixed boundaries.
The fundamental frequency depends on the length of the string, tension, and mass per unit length (linear mass density).
Integer multiples of the fundamental frequency (harmonics) can be excited as normal modes of vibration.

concept_notes.heading: Stationary Waves in Air Columns (Organ Pipes)
bullets: Open organ pipes have displacement antinodes at both open ends, producing all harmonics (even and odd).
Closed organ pipes have a displacement node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, producing only odd harmonics.
End correction accounts for the antinode forming slightly beyond the actual open boundary of the pipe.

derivations.title: Analytical Treatment of Stationary Waves
derivations.conditions: Two sinusoidal progressive waves of equal amplitude, frequency, and wavelength traveling in opposite directions.
steps: Let the incident wave be y_1 = A sin(omega t - kx) and the reflected wave traveling in the opposite direction be y_2 = A sin(omega t + kx).
By the principle of superposition, the resultant displacement is y = y_1 + y_2 = A [sin(omega t - kx) + sin(omega t + kx)].
Using the trigonometric identity sin(A - B) + sin(A + B) = 2 sin A cos B, obtain y = 2A cos(kx) sin(omega t).
derivations.result: y = [2A cos(kx)] sin(omega t), representing a stationary wave where amplitude depends on position x as A_s = 2A cos(kx).

derivations.title: Frequencies of Vibrating String Fixed at Both Ends
derivations.conditions: String of length L under tension T with linear mass density mu.
steps: Apply boundary conditions for a string of length L fixed at x = 0 and x = L, which implies nodes at both ends.
The condition for nodes at both ends requires L = n(lambda / 2), where n = 1, 2, 3, ...
Substitute lambda = v / f and velocity of transverse wave v = sqrt(T / mu) into the wavelength relation to solve for frequency f.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Displacement Profile of Stationary Waves
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A sinusoidal envelope showing standing wave loops with nodes (zero amplitude) and antinodes (maximum amplitude) labeled along a spatial x-axis.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows the spatial variation of vibration amplitude, demonstrating that nodes and antinodes maintain fixed spatial positions over time.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in identifying node-antinode counts and calculating wavelength from given length dimensions.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Melde's Experiment Setup
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A stretched string connected to an electrically driven tuning fork at one end and passing over a frictionless pulley to a mass hanger at the other end.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates transverse and longitudinal stationary wave modes in strings and relates frequency, tension, and linear mass density.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Numerical problems based on tuning fork frequency and resonance loops in parallel or perpendicular configurations.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Resonance Column Apparatus
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A cylindrical glass tube mounted vertically in a water reservoir, with a tuning fork held above the open mouth.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Used to determine the velocity of sound in air by finding resonant lengths corresponding to standing wave nodes and antinodes.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Direct questions on first and second resonance lengths and end correction calculations.

solved_numericals.question: A steel wire of length 1.0 m and mass 10 g is stretched with a tension of 400 N. Calculate the fundamental frequency of transverse vibrations of the wire.
solution_steps: Find the linear mass density mu = mass / length = 10 * 10^-3 kg / 1.0 m = 0.01 kg/m.
Calculate the wave velocity v = sqrt(T / mu) = sqrt(400 / 0.01) = sqrt(40000) = 200 m/s.
Calculate the fundamental frequency f_1 = v / (2L) = 200 / (2 * 1.0) = 100 Hz.

solved_numericals.question: Find the frequency of the third harmonic of an open organ pipe of length 0.5 m. Take the speed of sound in air as 340 m/s.
solution_steps: For an open organ pipe, the frequency of the n-th harmonic is given by f_n = n v / (2L).
Substitute n = 3, v = 340 m/s, and L = 0.5 m into the formula.

solved_numericals.question: A closed organ pipe and an open organ pipe have the same length. If the fundamental frequency of the open pipe is 300 Hz, calculate the fundamental frequency of the closed pipe, accounting for end correction by treating the effective length as L + 0.3d where diameter d = 0.02 L.
solution_steps: For the open pipe, fundamental frequency f_o = v / (2L_0) = 300 Hz.
For the closed pipe without end correction, fundamental frequency f_c = v / (4L_c). Since lengths are equal (L_0 = L_c = L), f_c = f_o / 2 = 150 Hz.
With end correction, effective length for open pipe is L_eff,o = L + 2(0.3d) = L + 0.6d, and for closed pipe is L_eff,c = L + 0.3d.
Since frequency is inversely proportional to effective length, f_c / f_o = L_eff,o / L_eff,c. Substitute d = 0.02 L to find the exact ratio and compute f_c.

assumptions_and_limitations: Amplitude of component waves is assumed to be identical; in real reflections, partial absorption causes unequal amplitudes, resulting in non-zero minimum displacement at nodes.
The string is assumed perfectly flexible with uniform cross-section and density, ignoring stiffness and bending rigidity.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Energy travels along a stationary wave from one node to the next.
common_misconceptions.correct: Energy is stationary and remains confined between adjacent nodes.
common_misconceptions.why: Nodes are points of zero displacement where no energy can flow across.

common_misconceptions.wrong: All particles in a stationary wave vibrate with the same amplitude.
common_misconceptions.correct: Amplitude varies continuously from zero at nodes to maximum at antinodes.
common_misconceptions.why: The spatial amplitude factor 2A cos(kx) depends on position x.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Closed organ pipes contain all harmonics like open pipes.
common_misconceptions.correct: Closed organ pipes contain only odd harmonics.
common_misconceptions.why: The boundary conditions (node at closed end, antinode at open end) exclude even integer multiples.

quick_revision: Stationary waves are formed by the superposition of two identical waves traveling in opposite directions with no net energy transport.
